flawed_step: The hypotheses “triangle-free” and “maximum degree at most 4” do not imply 3-colorability.
counterexample: Let G have vertices 0,...,11 and neighborhoods N(0)={1,4,6,9}, N(1)={0,2,5,7}, N(2)={1,3,6,8}, N(3)={2,4,7,9}, N(4)={0,3,5,8}, N(5)={1,4,10,11}, N(6)={0,2,10,11}, N(7)={1,3,8,11}, N(8)={2,4,7,10}, N(9)={0,3,10,11}, N(10)={5,6,8,9}, N(11)={5,6,7,9}. This is a simple 4-regular graph. Every displayed neighborhood is independent, so G is triangle-free. To see that G is not 3-colorable, label the colors A,B,C. Vertices 0,1,2,3,4 induce a 5-cycle. Up to permuting colors, set c(0)=A and c(1)=B; its five possible color patterns are ABABC, ABACB, ABCAB, ABCAC, and ABCBC. For ABABC, vertices 5,8,9 are forced to A,B,C, respectively, leaving their common neighbor 10 uncolorable. For ABACB, vertices 7,8,9 are forced to A,C,B; hence 10 is forced to A and 11 to C, while 5—adjacent to cycle vertices 1 and 4, both B—is left no color. For ABCAB, vertices 6,7,8 are forced to B,C,A; then 10 is forced to C and 5 to A, leaving 11 adjacent to vertices of all three colors. For ABCAC, vertices 5,6,7 are forced to A,B,C and have common neighbor 11. For ABCBC, vertices 5,6,9 are forced to A,B,C and have common neighbor 11. Thus every possible coloring of the 5-cycle fails to extend to a 3-coloring of G.
assessment_summary: The explicit 12-vertex graph is triangle-free, has maximum degree 4, and requires at least four colors, so it directly refutes the statement.
